claim: Measured end-to-end: on a slow wire (a job forced to cross between NVLink quads over PCIe), training throughput drops 3-5x versus the same job on NVSwitch or inside one quad, and the penalty is strategy-dependent — FSDP falls hardest because it communicates every layer, DDP holds up best because it communicates once per step.
stance_target: the repo's claim that DDP is the only viable training topology on a slow fabric, and that FSDP's extra communication is exposed rather than hidden
scope_conditions: Mistral-7B fine-tune on 4x H200, three wirings (NVSwitch, full NVL quad, cross-quad PCIe), DDP/ZeRO-1/2/3/FSDP, HuggingFace Accelerate defaults, BF16
quoted_support: The across-quads case is the cost of getting placement wrong. Throughput drops by 3 to 5x. ... FSDP falls the hardest, because it communicates every layer, and on a slow wire, those per-layer transfers can't hide behind compute. DDP holds up best because it communicates just once per step.

claim: Measured all-reduce bandwidth on identical H200 silicon: NVLink versus forced PCIe differs by ~10-11x, and the same four cards reach 322 GB/s inside an NVLink-bridged quad but only ~35 GB/s when the job spans two quads over PCIe — a ~9x difference decided purely by placement.
stance_target: the repo's claim that the fabric, not the algorithm, sets the ceiling on collective bandwidth
scope_conditions: H200 SXM (NVSwitch) and H200 NVL (two bridged quads of four) nodes; all-reduce microbenchmarks at 2/4/8 GPUs
quoted_support: The wire alone is worth about 10-11x. ... The same four cards, in the same node, run at 322 GB/s inside one quad and about 35 GB/s across two, a roughly 9x difference decided by nothing but which GPUs the job landed on.

claim: Measured all-reduce bandwidth scaling: NVSwitch stays flat and fast (330 GB/s at 2 GPUs to 467 GB/s at 8), an NVLink quad reaches 114 GB/s at 2 GPUs (only 6 of 18 links lit) and 322 GB/s at 4 (all 18 links lit), while cross-quad jobs sit at 28/35/39 GB/s at 2/4/8 GPUs and adding GPUs does not help.
stance_target: what all-reduce bandwidth looks like as a function of device count and topology, as a reference shape for the 5-GPU box
scope_conditions: H200 SXM and H200 NVL nodes; all-reduce at 2, 4 and 8 GPUs on three fabrics
quoted_support: NVSwitch stays flat and fast. 330 GB/s at two GPUs, rising gently to 467 at eight ... The NVL quad ... runs at about 114 GB/s, which is a third of the card's NVLink capacity ... a full quad reaches about 322 GB/s ... The third line is the cross quad case ... 28 GB/s at two GPUs, 35 at four, 39 at eight.

claim: Measured memory: Mistral-7B in BF16 with Adam needs 87 GB of model state per GPU (14 GB params + 14 GB gradients + ~58 GB fp32 optimizer states) before any activation, which OOMs on an 80 GB A100 under DDP; FSDP shards it to ~22 GB estimated and ~29 GB actual peak on 4 GPUs.
stance_target: the repo's claim that 7B fully trainable does not fit DDP on 64 GB cards
scope_conditions: Mistral-7B, BF16 mixed precision, Adam, 4x A100 80GB, HuggingFace Accelerate
quoted_support: The parameters take 14 GB: 7 billion of them, two bytes each. The gradients take another 14 GB. Then we have the optimizer states ... roughly 58 GB. Add it up, and we reach 87 GB before the model has seen a single batch ... DDP would need an estimated 87 GB per GPU for the model state ... FSDP shards this across 4 GPUs, bringing the estimated requirement down to about 22 GB per GPU. The actual peak during the run was about 29 GB.

claim: Measured peak memory across the sharding dial for the same 7B job on 4 GPUs: DDP 87 GB, ZeRO-1 55 GB, ZeRO-2 51 GB, ZeRO-3 40 GB, FSDP 37 GB — and it never reaches 87/4 = 22 GB because activations are still produced independently on every GPU.
stance_target: the repo's claim that sharding model state does not remove activation memory, which is why the frozen-Engram trick targets parameters rather than activations
scope_conditions: Mistral-7B on 4x A100 80GB, BF16, HuggingFace Accelerate DeepSpeed defaults
quoted_support: Those are the measured peaks for Mistral-7B on four GPUs, and they fall in a clean pattern as you move down the dial. 87 GB at DDP, then 55, 51, 40, and 37 GB. But notice it never drops to a quarter of 87 GB ... The floor is mostly activations and runtime overhead.

claim: Measured throughput on a fast wire: ZeRO-1 and ZeRO-2 lose about 20% of DDP's throughput, ZeRO-3 loses more, but FSDP — sharding exactly what ZeRO-3 shards — claws nearly all of it back at about the same memory; on a slow wire the dial flattens and all stages converge to the same low throughput.
stance_target: whether a milder ZeRO stage can buy back throughput on a slow fabric (answer: no)
scope_conditions: Mistral-7B on 4x H200, NVSwitch vs cross-quad PCIe, HuggingFace Accelerate defaults (untuned DeepSpeed config)
quoted_support: On the fast wire, the middle of the dial loses. ZeRO-1 and ZeRO-2 give up around 20% of DDP's throughput, and ZeRO-3 gives up more. But FSDP, sharding the same things as ZeRO-3, claws nearly all of that throughput back while using about the same memory. ... On a slow wire, the dial flattens.

claim: Measured on models that fit: FSDP uses ~4.5x less memory than DDP (0.39 vs 1.79 GB for DINOv2-base, 1.39 vs 6.26 GB for DINOv2-large) but DDP is only ~4-6% faster, so when the model fits replicated the memory saving is not worth the communication.
stance_target: the repo's claim that DDP is the right default when the model fits, and FSDP only earns its cost when it must
scope_conditions: DINOv2 base (86M) and large (304M) on Food-101, 4x A100 80GB, batch 32/256 per GPU, BF16
quoted_support: FSDP uses significantly less memory per GPU: 0.39 GB vs. 1.79 GB for the base model, and 1.39 GB vs. 6.26 GB for the large model. That is roughly 4.5x less memory with FSDP. ... DDP is consistently faster, around 6% higher throughput for the base model and 4% for the large one.

claim: Reference link rates quoted: a PCIe Gen5 x16 slot moves ~64 GB/s in one direction, while an H200 GPU's 18 NVLink links give ~450 GB/s per direction, about 7x a single PCIe slot.
stance_target: the per-link bandwidth scale against which the CMP 170HX box's Gen2 x4 (~2 GB/s theoretical per direction) should be placed
scope_conditions: PCIe Gen5 x16; H100/H200 NVLink (18 links)
quoted_support: A PCIe Gen5 x16 slot moves somewhere around 64 GB/s in one direction. ... On an H100 or H200, each GPU has 18 NVLink connections, which together come to roughly 450 GB/s in each direction, about 7x what a single PCIe slot provides.

claim: The fabric cannot be inferred from the GPU model name — two H200 nodes with identical cards behave completely differently — and the diagnostic is a single command, nvidia-smi topo -m, which is the same pre-flight the repo prescribes via lspci -vv.
stance_target: the repo's pre-flight requirement to measure the negotiated link before trusting any throughput estimate
scope_conditions: H200 SXM vs H200 NVL nodes; single-node fabrics
quoted_support: you cannot infer the GPU-to-GPU fabric from the GPU model name alone. You have to look at the topology. ... So before launching a distributed job, run one command: nvidia-smi topo -m.

claim: The article's 87 GB figure implies ~12.4 bytes/param, not the ZeRO paper's 16 bytes/param, because it omits the fp32 master weight copy — so the repo's '~112 GB per card' for a fully trainable 7B is the conservative (master-copy-included) number and 87 GB is the floor without it.
stance_target: the exact per-parameter memory constant behind the repo's 112 GB claim
scope_conditions: Mistral-7B BF16 Adam accounting; comparison with ZeRO mixed-precision accounting (arXiv 1910.02054)
quoted_support: The parameters take 14 GB ... The gradients take another 14 GB ... roughly 58 GB. Add it up, and we reach 87 GB before the model has seen a single batch or a single activation has been computed.
